docs.title: Federated Node - Documentation
docs.text:
2.x beta. This documentation covers the 2.x Federated Node, which is in beta.

This documentation covers deploying, setting up, testing, and using the PHEMS Federated Node (FN) 2.x.

docs.title: What is the Federated Node?
docs.text:
The Federated Node lets researchers run analytical tasks against sensitive datasets without the data ever leaving your institution. Analytics code (packaged as a Docker container) is sent to the data - not the other way around. Only the results come out, as a pull request that someone at your institution reviews before it is merged.

It deploys as a Helm chart onto a Kubernetes cluster. Tasks are asked for with a pull request, so nothing has to call into your node to start one.

Core components bundled in the chart:

  • nexus-api - the FN API (FastAPI). It keeps the record of everything and decides what is allowed
  • Dagster - polls the git repositories, starts task pods, and delivers results
  • Keycloak - logins and the admin role
  • Traefik - reverse proxy and ingress (recommended for production)
  • PostgreSQL - FN metadata (projects, tasks, results) - you provide this externally in production

You also need a git host for the trigger and results repositories: GitHub (with a GitHub App) or Gitea. The chart can run a Gitea for development only.

docs.title: How a task runs
docs.text:
1. A researcher adds a small JSON file (the task spec: which image to run, which dataset) to the project's trigger repository, in a pull request.
  2. Someone at the institution merges it.
  3. The node sees the merged pull request, turns it into a task, and starts a pod in your cluster with the researcher's image, next to the dataset.
  4. When the task finishes, the node pushes the result files to the project's results repository as a branch and opens a pull request.
  5. Someone at the institution reviews that pull request. Merging it is the release of the results.
sequenceDiagram
    participant Researcher
    participant Trigger as Trigger Repo
    participant DataController as Data Controller
    participant Node as Federated Node
    participant Task as Task Pod
    participant Results as Results Repo

    Researcher->>Trigger: Raise PR (task spec: image + dataset)
    DataController->>Trigger: Approve PR
    DataController->>Trigger: Merge PR
    Node->>Trigger: Poll merged PRs, read the task spec
    Node->>Node: Create task, check the project, dataset and repos are allowed
    Node->>Task: Start pod in the tasks namespace, next to the dataset
    Task-->>Node: Write results to its output folder
    Node->>Results: Push results branch, open Results PR
    DataController->>Results: Approve Results PR
    DataController->>Results: Merge Results PR
    Node->>Results: Sync PR state, record the result as merged

Architecture explains each part. Researcher guide shows the researcher's side.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Understanding how it fits together: Architecture covers the components, the flow, and the decisions you need to make yourself before production.

Deploying for the first time: Prerequisites, then Deploy: Core with the guide for your platform, then Post-deploy testing. The platform guides are Azure (AKS), AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and On-Premises.

Running tasks as a researcher: Researcher guide.

Building an analytics container: Analytics container development covers the environment variables, where to write results, and what the pod is and is not allowed to do.

Registering the databases tasks read from: Datasets.

Looking after a running node: Operations.

What changed in each release is in the release notes.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: How to look after a running Federated Node 2.x: start the sensors, switch things on and off, check that it is healthy, and work out why a pull request did nothing.

docs.title: Start the sensors
docs.text:
Every Dagster sensor starts stopped, so nothing is polled and no task runs until you start them. Do it once the first project is enabled. The order does not matter, and after a reinstall you start them again.

With the API (admin):

curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/dagster/sensors" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"status": "RUNNING"}' | jq
curl -sS "$FN/dagster/sensors" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq        # every sensor, its status and latest tick

With the Dagster UI. It has no login, so reach it by port-forward and never publish it:

kubectl port-forward -n federated-node svc/federatednode-dagster-webserver 3000:80

Open http://localhost:3000, go to Automation, and turn on all twelve sensors.

The sensors, by group:

Group Sensors Job ingest git_pull_request_ingest_sensor Polls each trigger repository once and stores new merged pull requests evaluate git_pull_request_evaluate_sensor Turns each stored pull request into a task, or rejects it with a cause launcher task_launcher_sensor Starts a Dagster run for each pending task status five run-status sensors, task_reconcile_sensor Copy the run's status onto the task delivery task_results_delivery_sensor, results_pull_request_sync_sensor, results_delivery_retry_sensor Push results, track the results pull request, retry failures

How often they tick is the chart value fnDagster.sensors.minIntervalSeconds (30 seconds by default), and how long a failed run waits before a retry is retryIntervalSeconds (60 seconds). To pause the node, stop the sensors the same way, with {"status": "STOPPED"}.

docs.title: Switch things on and off
docs.text:
Two flags sit on every resource. Enabled is a switch anyone allowed to manage the resource can flip. Revoked is admin only and takes effect at once. A resource is active only when it is enabled and not revoked, and only active ones are used.

To stop Do this A whole project PATCH /projects/<id> with {"enabled": false}, or {"revoked": true} (admin) One project's use of one resource PATCH the assignment: /projects/<id>/datasets/<dataset_id>, /projects/<id>/repositories/triggers/<id>, /projects/<id>/repositories/results/<id> A resource for every project PATCH /global/datasets/<id>, /global/repositories/triggers/<id>, /global/repositories/results/<id> or /global/providers/<id> with enabled or revoked A credential PATCH /global/secrets/<label>. Disabling it also disables the datasets and repositories that use it, and moves its value to the quarantine namespace. They stay off when you turn the secret back on

What happens to work in flight:

  • The launcher fails a pending task, with the cause in its state_cause, when anything it uses is revoked or deleted.
  • A result for a revoked or deleted results repository is recorded as REVOKED and nothing is delivered.
  • A result for a disabled one is retried once it is switched back on.

DELETE is a soft delete: the record leaves the API, its assignments go with it, and the name is free again. Deleting a dataset or repository that projects still use is a 409 listing them. The full table of what each state does is in the repo's revoke-and-enabled.md.

docs.title: Checking on it
docs.text: Question Where to look Can everything be reached? GET /global/healthcheck, GET /projects/<id>/healthcheck, and per resource GET /global/datasets/<id>/healthcheck, /global/secrets/<label>/healthcheck, /global/providers/<id>/healthcheck, /global/repositories/triggers/<id>/healthcheck, /global/repositories/results/<id>/healthcheck What is this project doing? GET /projects/<id>/tasks Is a run stuck or failing? The Dagster UI, Runs, for the logs of each step Are the sensors running? GET /dagster/sensors, or the Dagster UI Automation page Whole-node checklist The repo's deploy and health checklist

docs.title: Reading a run
docs.text: Open the Dagster UI by port-forward (above), and go to Runs. A task's run is tagged with the task's id. Its logs show each step, including whatever the container wrote to stdout and stderr.

docs.title: A pull request was merged and nothing happened
docs.text: Cause How you see it Sensors are stopped (the default) GET /dagster/sensors: STOPPED The project is disabled, or an assignment is inactive The project or assignment shows enabled false or revoked true The pull request does not add a .json file under watch_dir, or targets another branch No trigger is made for that project (it is skipped and logged) It was merged before the trigger repository was assigned or the project enabled Skipped by design. Enable with backfill, or merge a new one It adds more than one spec file, or the spec is not valid The trigger is REJECTED and state_cause says why A token is wrong or expired The resource's healthcheck fails and names it. Rotate it with PATCH /global/secrets/<label> The task stays pending state_cause on the task: usually the dataset assignment is inactive or its secret is disabled. Fix the cause, then POST /projects/<id>/tasks/<task_id>/retry The task starts but its container cannot reach the database The container times out connecting. The database is outside the private address ranges and not in taskNetworkPolicy.datasetEgress (Deploy: Core)

docs.title: Results not delivered
docs.text: A succeeded task whose results do not appear: check the task's results (GET /projects/<id>/tasks/<task_id>/results). A failed delivery shows its error and is retried by the delivery sensors. The usual causes are a results zip over 10 MiB (fnDagster.results.maxZipBytes) and a token without write access to the results repository. A task that failed delivers nothing.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The per-run folders on the shared results volume are not removed after delivery. Watch the volume's size.
  • A result over the size cap has no other route: it fails.
  • The Dagster UI has no login. Reach it only by port-forward.

The repo's known issues list the details.

docs.title: Post-Deploy Testing
docs.text: Use this guide to verify your Federated Node 2.x is healthy before you set up a project and hand it over to users. It checks the install only.

docs.title: 1. Check pod status
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n federated-node
kubectl get pods -n keycloak
kubectl get jobs -A

Every pod should reach Running, and the *-db-init and keycloak-realm-init jobs should show Completed. The first start takes a few minutes while Keycloak and the databases initialise.

If anything is stuck, check its logs:

kubectl describe pod <pod> -n federated-node
kubectl logs <pod> -n federated-node

docs.title: 2. Set your hostname
docs.text:
All examples in this guide use $FN_HOST.

If accessing via a public hostname: 

export FN_HOST=https://fn.your-institution.example.com

If port-forwarding to nexus-api directly (no Traefik): 

kubectl port-forward -n federated-node service/nexus-api 5000:5000
export FN_HOST=http://localhost:5000

docs.title: 3. Health check
docs.text:
curl "$FN_HOST/health_check"

It returns "status": "ok" when nexus-api can reach Keycloak, and a 502 otherwise. If it stays at 502, give Keycloak a minute and retry, then check the Keycloak pod's logs.

docs.title: 4. Login
docs.text:
Log in as the first user, with the email from firstUserSecret.email and the password in the secret you created for it. /login takes form fields, not JSON, and returns a bearer token:

PASSWORD=$(kubectl get secret -n federated-node fn-first-user -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d)

TOKEN=$(curl --silent "$FN_HOST/login" \
    -F "username=admin@your-institution.example.com" \
    -F "password=$PASSWORD" | jq -r '.token')

The token lasts 8 hours (POST /refresh_token renews it). The Keycloak admin password, if you need it, is in the kc-secrets secret in the keycloak namespace.

Then check the node as a whole:

curl -sS "$FN_HOST/global/healthcheck" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq

A failing check shows in the body with a status of 200, never a 500, and never contains a secret value. On a new node with nothing registered yet, it has little to check.

docs.title: 5. Check Dagster
docs.text:
The Dagster UI has no login and no route, so reach it with a port-forward. It listens on port 80, so 3000:3000 fails:

kubectl port-forward -n federated-node svc/federatednode-dagster-webserver 3000:80

Open http://localhost:3000 and check that the code location loads with no error. Under Automation you should see twelve sensors, all stopped. That is how a new node starts.

docs.title: 6. Register a test dataset
docs.text:
A dataset registration tells the node where a research database lives. The node stores the connection details and never copies the data. This step proves the node can reach a database from inside the cluster. Use a database you have, with a login that can read it. The full list of fields and types is in Datasets.

Store the login as a secret (the keys are USERNAME and PASSWORD), then register the dataset:

AUTH=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json")

curl -sS -X POST "$FN_HOST/global/secrets" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "label": "test-dataset-creds",
  "provider": "K8S",
  "values": {"USERNAME": "db-user", "PASSWORD": "db-password"}
}' | jq

DATASET_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN_HOST/global/datasets" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "name": "test_dataset",
  "host": "your-database-host.example.com",
  "port": 5432,
  "type": "postgres",
  "secret_label": "test-dataset-creds",
  "read_schema": "public"
}' | jq -r '.id')

curl -sS "$FN_HOST/global/datasets/$DATASET_ID/healthcheck" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

The healthcheck connects to the database with the stored login. A failure is reported in the body, with a status of 200. If it fails, the message says why: a wrong host or port, a wrong login, or a cluster firewall in between. The healthcheck covers PostgreSQL and SQL Server datasets.

If you registered a throwaway dataset, remove it so the name is free: DELETE /global/datasets/$DATASET_ID, and then DELETE /global/secrets/test-dataset-creds?force=true. Without force the secret is refused while an enabled dataset still uses it.

Whether a task can reach the database is a separate question, because task pods are limited by the network policy. A database on a private address works by default. For any other address, list it in taskNetworkPolicy.datasetEgress (Deploy: Core).

docs.title: 7. Run the chart's own tests
docs.text:
helm test federatednode -n federated-node --logs

With smoketests: true in your values, the tests also create and delete real rows. The full list of checks for a node is the repo's deploy and health checklist.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Datasets: register the databases tasks will read from.
  • Set up a project: its repositories, its dataset, and the sensors. The repo's MANAGEMENT.md walks through it.
  • Researcher guide: how a researcher asks for a task, once the project is enabled.
  • Operations: looking after a running node.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before deploying the Federated Node 2.x, make sure the following are in place.

docs.title: Required tools
docs.text:
Tool Purpose Install guide kubectl Interact with your Kubernetes cluster docs.kubernetes.io helm (v3+) Deploy the FN chart helm.sh/docs/intro/install jq Parse API responses in shell examples stedolan.github.io/jq

An example values.yaml is in Deploy: Core, and the platform guides add the storage, ingress and certificate settings for each platform.

docs.title: Kubernetes cluster
docs.text:
Any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster works. Each platform has its own guide with its prerequisites and known issues:

  • Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
  • AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)
  • Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
  • On-premises (RKE2, k3s, kubeadm)

Size the cluster for the base pods plus your analytics task pods. Start with 4 vCPU and 8 GB RAM per node. A task pod gets 500m CPU and 1 GiB of memory by default and may use up to 2 CPU and 4 GiB, and a task spec may ask for up to 4 CPU and 16 GiB. These are taskCompute.default and taskCompute.max, so size your nodes for the number of tasks you expect to run at once.

The cluster's network plugin (CNI) must enforce NetworkPolicy: Calico, Cilium, or your cloud's network policy add-on. The chart denies a task pod all traffic except cluster DNS, the private address ranges in taskNetworkPolicy.privateEgress and the dataset databases you list in taskNetworkPolicy.datasetEgress. On a CNI that ignores NetworkPolicy, that rule does nothing.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
The FN needs a PostgreSQL server that the cluster can reach, with an admin login. It needs its own databases on it (fn_nexus for nexus-api, keycloak_db and dagster), not your research data. By default the chart creates them and their roles for you, and nexus-api creates its tables on first start.

Have ready the hostname, the port, and the admin login and password. On a managed service (Azure, RDS, Cloud SQL) the admin is not called postgres: you set it in db.superuser. If the server requires TLS, set db.enforceSSL.

If a DBA owns the databases and you have no admin login, the chart can instead use roles and databases that already exist. Deploy: Core covers both.

Back up Keycloak's database as well as nexus-api's. They are separate databases on the same server. Restoring only nexus-api's gives you a node that knows its datasets and projects but has lost every login.

docs.title: Shared storage
docs.text:
Task pods and Dagster's run pods write results to the same volume, so it must be ReadWriteMany. ReadWriteOnce disks do not work. Supported backends:

  • Azure Files - for AKS
  • AWS EFS - for EKS (the EFS CSI driver and an access point are needed)
  • NFS - cloud-agnostic, on-prem friendly. On GKE, use Filestore
  • Local host path - single node and development only

The choice is made at install time and is awkward to change later, because it means recreating the volumes. The per-run result folders are not removed after delivery, so size the volume for the output of every run you expect to keep.

docs.title: A hostname and a certificate
docs.text: The node needs a DNS name pointing at Traefik, and a TLS certificate for it. Either create the certificate yourself, or have cert-manager get and renew one. The chart's own cert-manager issuer covers Azure DNS and Route 53. Your platform guide says what to do elsewhere.

docs.title: A git host and two repositories
docs.text:
Tasks are asked for through git, so every project needs a trigger repository and a results repository. They can be the same repository, as long as the directories used for each do not overlap. They must already exist: the node does not create them. Use either:

  • GitHub, with a GitHub App installed on the repositories (read and write on Contents and Pull requests).
  • Gitea, with an OAuth2 application for the admin user.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
Outbound HTTPS to ghcr.io (images), to your git host (api.github.com for GitHub), and to wherever your analytics images live. If the cluster has no internet egress, mirror the FN images and your analytics images into an internal registry.

Nothing needs to call into the node to start a task. Admins who use the API reach nexus-api over HTTPS through Traefik, so one address must be reachable from their workstations or VPN.

docs.title: Install the Gateway API and Traefik CRDs
docs.text:
If you use the chart's Traefik (traefik.enabled: true, recommended for production), two sets of Kubernetes CRDs must exist before helm install. The chart refuses to install without them, and says so. This is a one-time step per cluster. From a checkout of the repository:

./scripts/gateway-api-installer.sh

It applies the Gateway API CRDs (version 1.4.0 unless you pass another) and the Traefik CRDs, with server-side apply. Skip this only if you set traefik.enabled: false and bring your own ingress.

docs.title: Notes on secrets
docs.text:
Credentials are Kubernetes secrets, not values in your values.yaml. The chart creates most of them (database passwords, Keycloak credentials, the Dagster login). Deploy: Core lists the few you have to create.

A few characters cause problems in shell --from-literal commands: " must be escaped as \", and % needs special handling. When in doubt, use a YAML manifest and pre-encode the value with echo -n "yourvalue" | base64.

Create the namespace before the secrets. Secrets created in the wrong namespace are not visible to the FN pods:

kubectl create namespace federated-node

Git and dataset credentials are not Helm secrets. You register them through the API after the install, as global secrets.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
Follow Deploy: Core, which covers the steps common to every platform, and add the guide for your platform alongside it:

  • Deploy: Azure (AKS)
  • Deploy: AWS (EKS)
  • Deploy: GCP (GKE)
  • Deploy: On-Premises

docs.title: Researcher Guide
docs.text:
This guide is for researchers who want to run an analysis on a Federated Node 2.x. You do not call the node to start a task. You write a small JSON file, add it to the project's trigger repository in a pull request, and when someone at the institution merges it, the node runs your container next to the data. The results come back as another pull request.

Before you start, ask the node's admin for:

  • the trigger repository, its watch directory and its base branch (where your spec file goes);
  • the name of the dataset you may use, or whether the project has a default;
  • where the results repository is, so you can find your results.

You also need a container image that follows the container contract, pushed somewhere the cluster can pull it from.

docs.title: 1. Write the task spec
docs.text:
The spec file says what to run. Only spec and metadata are allowed at the top level, and spec is required:

{
  "spec": {
    "image": "ghcr.io/your-org/your-analytics-image:1.0",
    "dataset": "my-dataset",
    "env": {"COHORT": "paediatric", "MIN_AGE": "0"},
    "tags": {"team": "analytics"},
    "config": {"epochs": 3},
    "compute": {
      "requests": {"cpu": "500m", "memory": "1Gi"},
      "limits": {"cpu": "2", "memory": "4Gi"}
    }
  },
  "metadata": {"ticket": "ABC-1"}
}
Field Required What it does spec.image yes The container image to run, up to 256 characters. spec.dataset no The name of a dataset your project has and that is switched on. Without it, the project's default dataset is used, if it has one. spec.env no Environment variables for your container. See below. spec.tags no Text labels copied onto the task's run. spec.config no A JSON object your container reads as a file, at the path in CONFIG_PATH. Its contents are not checked. spec.compute no The CPU and memory to ask for: requests and limits, each with an optional cpu and memory. metadata no Yours: any JSON, not checked, kept with the task and delivered with the results.

Any other field, at either level, makes the pull request REJECTED.

env:

  • A name matches ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ and arrives upper-cased.
  • Values reach your container as text. Send strings: a JSON true arrives as True.
  • You cannot set ARTIFACT_PATH, CDM_SCHEMA, WRITE_SCHEMA, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, CONNECTION_STRING or CONFIG_PATH, or any name starting with DAGSTER_ or KUBERNETES_, in any letter case. The node sets those itself.
  • All of env, as JSON, is at most 32 KiB.

tags: a key is 1 to 63 letters, digits, _, . or - (so no /), and a value is text.

compute: values are Kubernetes quantities (500m, 2, 512Mi, 4Gi). A limit cannot be lower than its request, and nothing can be over the node's maximum. A request with no limit of its own cannot be over the node's default limit. Without compute, the node's defaults apply. Ask your admin for the numbers (taskCompute in the chart).

The whole file is at most 64 KiB. The exact rules are in the spec schema, which your editor can use to check the file.

docs.title: 2. Open and merge the pull request
docs.text:
1. In the trigger repository, on a branch, add the spec file under the watch directory, for example specs/first-task.json.
  2. Open a pull request into the base branch.
  3. Someone with merge rights merges it. Only merged pull requests are read.

What the node does with a merged pull request:

The pull request Result Adds exactly one .json file under the watch directory, with a valid spec A task is created Adds more than one .json file under the watch directory REJECTED: "Several new spec files" Adds one, but the spec is not valid REJECTED, with the reason Adds no .json file under the watch directory, or goes to another branch Ignored: no task, no error Was merged before your project was enabled Ignored, unless the admin asked for a backfill

Only added files count. Changing or deleting a spec file does nothing, and editing a spec after it is merged changes nothing: the task keeps the spec as read at the merge. To run again with changes, add a new file in a new pull request.

The task is named <project name>:PR#<pull request number>.

docs.title: 3. Wait for the task
docs.text:
The node checks for new pull requests every 30 seconds or so, then queues the task and starts a pod. The task goes through PENDING, QUEUED, RUNNING and then SUCCESS or FAILED (CANCELED if it is stopped). Your admin can see the run and its logs in Dagster, and can read the task through the API (GET /projects/<id>/tasks).

If nothing seems to happen after a few minutes, the usual causes are on the admin's side: the sensors are stopped, the project or one of its resources is switched off, or your pull request was one of the ignored kinds above. A rejected pull request or a task that cannot start has its reason in state_cause.

A task that fails delivers nothing. The container must exit with status 0 to succeed.

docs.title: 4. Get your results
docs.text:
When the task succeeds, the node pushes the results to the project's results repository and opens a results pull request from a new branch into the project's results base_branch. Under the project's target_dir, the branch and the files are laid out like this:

<target_dir>/<trigger repository name>/<pr number>/<task id>/
    results.zip     everything your container wrote to ARTIFACT_PATH
    spec.json       your spec file, byte for byte (so your metadata rides along)
    run.json        the node, project, trigger, task and delivery details

The branch is named <target_dir>/<trigger repository name>/<pr number>/<task id>-<merge commit sha, first 7>.

The results.zip can be at most 10 MiB (the node's setting fnDagster.results.maxZipBytes). Over that, the delivery fails. Symbolic links in your output are skipped. The structure of run.json is in the run schema.

The results pull request is the review step. Someone at the institution reads it, and merging it releases the results. Closing it without merging does not. The node records which happened.

The outcome is not commented back on your trigger pull request, so look in the results repository.

docs.title: Trying it
docs.text: On a development node with the chart's Gitea, fncli open-pr --merge opens and merges a sample pull request for you. The spec file it commits has the format described here.

docs.title: Using the API
docs.text:
This guide covers everyday interactions with the nexus-api of a Federated Node 2.x: logging in, what the routes are for, and the conventions they share. A researcher does not need the API to run a task: see the Researcher guide.

Every node serves its own interactive reference at /docs, for example https://fn.your-institution.example.com/docs, and the same description as openapi.json (also in the repo's nexus/api folder). Treat those as the source of truth for request and response bodies.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: export FN=https://fn.your-institution.example.com

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
/login takes form fields, not JSON, and returns a bearer token:

TOKEN=$(curl --silent "$FN/login" \
    -F "username=your@email.com" \
    -F "password=yourpassword" | jq -r '.token')

AUTH=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json")

Tokens are valid for 8 hours by default (the chart value token.life).

docs.title: Refresh a token
docs.text: curl --silent -X POST "$FN/refresh_token" "${AUTH[@]}"

docs.title: The routes
docs.text:
Area Routes Who Health GET /health_check, GET /ready_check No login needed Login POST /login, POST /refresh_token Anyone with an account Global resources /global/secrets, /global/providers, /global/datasets, /global/repositories/triggers, /global/repositories/results Admin to create, change and revoke Users /global/users Admin Projects /projects, /projects/<id> Admin to create Assignments /projects/<id>/datasets, .../secrets, .../repositories/triggers, .../repositories/results Admin Tasks and results /projects/<id>/tasks, /projects/<id>/results Task rights. GET /tasks (every task) is admin Sensors /dagster/sensors Admin Health checks GET .../healthcheck on the node, a project, and each resource Admin

The pattern for each kind of resource is the same: GET lists or reads, POST creates (globals), PUT assigns (to a project), PATCH changes, DELETE removes. The id in the URL of an assignment is the global resource's id, not the assignment's.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Enabled and revoked. Every resource has an enabled flag, which anyone allowed to manage it can flip, and a revoked flag, which is admin only and takes effect at once. Only a resource that is enabled and not revoked is used. See Operations.
  • Soft delete. DELETE hides the record and frees its name. A resource that projects still use gives a 409 that lists them.
  • Health checks. A failing check is reported in the response body with a status of 200, never a 500, and never contains a secret value.
  • Secrets are write-only. No call returns a secret's values or even its key names.
  • Unknown fields. Some create bodies (a dataset, for example) ignore fields they do not know, so read a record back after creating it.
  • Bad input. An invalid request body is a 400. A move a record's state does not allow is a 409.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Logins are Keycloak users. An admin creates and lists them through the API:

# Create a user. The response shows a temporary password, once.
curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/users" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "email": "researcher@your-institution.example.com",
  "firstName": "Ada",
  "lastName": "Researcher",
  "role": "Users"
}' | jq

# List users, with their roles and whether they still have to set a password
curl -sS "$FN/global/users" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

Only email is required. username defaults to the email, and role to Users. A user that already exists is a 400.

The new user changes the temporary password with PUT /global/users/reset-password and the body {"email": "...", "tempPassword": "...", "newPassword": "..."}, which needs no login.

The node's roles are realm roles in Keycloak:

Role Used for Users A basic login. Researchers do not need one in the common case: they work in git. Administrator Registers and revokes the global resources, creates users, and manages projects. Super Administrator Everything an Administrator can do, plus the wider Keycloak realm permissions. System Integrations. Dagster logs in to nexus-api as a system user.

The first admin is created at install time from firstUserSecret (Deploy: Core).

docs.title: Datasets, repositories, projects
docs.text:
These are covered where you set them up:

  • Dataset fields and checks: Datasets.
  • Switching things on and off: Operations.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A task is normally created by a merged pull request, so there is no "submit" call to learn: see Researcher guide. Through the API you look at tasks and manage them (admin):

# The tasks of a project, with their status
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# One task
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# The pull request that created it
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID/trigger" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# Its results delivery
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID/results" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# Queue a failed or canceled task for another attempt
curl -sS -X POST "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID/retry" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

A task's status is PENDING, QUEUED, RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELED. The reason a task cannot start or a pull request was rejected is in state_cause.

Read a run's logs in the Dagster UI (Operations).

POST /projects/<id>/tasks creates a task without a pull request, but results delivery is built around the pull request, so such a task has no results delivery. Use a pull request.

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text:
Nothing runs until the Dagster sensors are started. As an admin, start and stop them from the API:

# Start every sensor
curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/dagster/sensors" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"status": "RUNNING"}' | jq

# Stop one
curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/dagster/sensors/task_launcher_sensor" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"status": "STOPPED"}' | jq

GET /dagster/sensors lists each sensor with its status and its latest tick. See Operations.
